issues.legal_issue: An accomplice’s testimony may support a conviction when it is reliable and independently corroborated in material particulars connecting each accused with the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on testimony from a participant in the crimes who testified as an approver.
The approver’s account of the crimes and the accused persons’ involvement was supported by eyewitnesses, witnesses to surrounding circumstances, recoveries, and other evidence.
The court found the approver’s testimony reliable and sufficient corroboration as to the accused persons implicated.
issues.conclusion: The approver’s testimony, with the corroboration found in this case, supported the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 133 of the Evidence Act, a conviction based on uncorroborated accomplice testimony is not illegal; however, the practice reflected in illustration (b) to Section 114 is to seek corroboration. The testimony must be reliable and corroborated in material particulars so as to connect the accused with the crime, but corroboration need not independently establish every circumstance or be sufficient by itself to convict. The court relied on Swaran Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Lachhi Ram v. State of Punjab, Mohd. Hussain v. State, Ravindra Singh v. State of Punjab, Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, Tribhuvan Nath v. State of Maharashtra, and Vemireddy Satyanarayan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.accomplice_testimony_reliable: A participant in the crime gave testimony that the court found reliable.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration_conne: Independent evidence corroborated material parts of the testimony and connected the accused with the crime.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal involves reliable accomplice testimony and independent material evidence connecting the accused with the crime, the testimony can support the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A retracted judicial confession may support a conviction when it was voluntary and true and receives sufficient independent corroboration in material particulars.
material_facts: Two accused made judicial confessions before magistrates after the required precautions and opportunities for reflection.
The court found the confessions voluntary and true despite their later retraction.
Witness testimony, surrounding circumstances, and recoveries corroborated material aspects of the confessions, including the crimes and the accused persons’ participation.
issues.conclusion: The retracted confessions, which the court found voluntary, true, and materially corroborated, supported the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: A judicial confession must be voluntary and true. Although it is not illegal to convict on an uncorroborated confession, prudence requires corroboration before acting on a retracted confession; general corroboration of important incidents in material particulars is sufficient and need not independently establish every detail or itself be enough for conviction. The court relied on Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, Swaran Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Boota Singh.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and judicial_confession_retracted and confession_voluntary_and_true and independent_material_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.judicial_confession_retracted: An accused made a judicial confession and later withdrew or disowned it.
predicates.confession_voluntary_and_true: The court found that the confession was voluntary and true.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration: Independent evidence corroborated important parts of the confession in material particulars.

issues.definition: A retracted judicial confession can support a conviction when it is found voluntary and true and independent evidence corroborates its important material aspects.

issues.legal_issue: The marital-communications privilege does not bar testimony by a person who was living as a partner but was not legally married to the accused.
material_facts: A witness testified about statements and events involving the accused.
The witness was living with the accused as his mistress, while his existing marriage remained in force.
The court found that the witness was not legally married to the accused.
issues.conclusion: The privilege for communications between spouses did not prevent the witness’s testimony from being used against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Section 122 of the Evidence Act does not apply to communications between persons who were not legally married to each other; the court therefore treated the witness as a mistress rather than a spouse for this purpose.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The evidence is being considered in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.witness_not_legally_married_to_accused: The witness and the accused were not legally married to each other.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, the marital-communications privilege is unavailable when the witness was not legally married to the accused.

issues.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified only in an exceptional murder case after balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances concerning both the crime and the offender.
material_facts: The court found that two leading participants were responsible for multiple planned, brutal and gruesome murders committed as part of organized criminal activity.
The victims were helpless, and the perpetrators concealed or disposed of the bodies to screen the crimes.
The court considered the offenders’ roles and the arguments advanced as mitigating circumstances, but found the crimes exceptionally grave and the offenders a menace to society.
issues.conclusion: The court confirmed the death sentences for the two leading participants, finding the case to be among the rarest of rare cases and the alternative of life imprisonment inadequate.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 354(3) and 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure require death to be an exceptional sentence: the court must consider aggravating and mitigating circumstances, pay due regard to both the crime and the criminal, and impose death only when the alternative is unquestionably foreclosed. The court relied on Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P., Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), Mangal Singh v. State of U.P., and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: capital_sentencing_appeal and multiple_planned_brutal_murders and offender_led_or_actively_drove_crimes and aggravating_circumstances_overwhelm_mitigation and life_sentence_inadequate

predicates.capital_sentencing_appeal: The case is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.multiple_planned_brutal_murders: The offender was involved in multiple murders that were planned and carried out with exceptional brutality.
predicates.offender_led_or_actively_drove_crimes: The offender led or actively drove the criminal activity that resulted in the murders.
predicates.aggravating_circumstances_overwhelm_miti: The court found the aggravating circumstances outweighed the mitigating circumstances after considering both the crimes and the offender.
predicates.life_sentence_inadequate: The court found that a life sentence would be inadequate in light of the offender’s conduct and the gravity of the crimes.

issues.definition: In a capital-sentencing appeal, an offender who drove multiple planned and exceptionally brutal murders may receive the death sentence only when the aggravating circumstances overwhelm mitigation and a life sentence is inadequate.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence is not justified for an offender when the evidence about that offender’s individual role is not of sufficient quality to establish the exceptional culpability required for that sentence.
material_facts: The offender’s convictions for participating in the murders were supported by the accomplice’s testimony and corroborating evidence establishing common intention.
The evidence about the offender’s particular actions in two murders came from the accomplice, whose account contained a discrepancy about the offender’s role.
The other convicted participants’ retracted confessions implicated the offender but could not be used to assess the nature of his individual participation for sentencing.
The court distinguished this offender’s evidence and role from those of the two leading participants.
issues.conclusion: The court upheld the offender’s convictions but reduced the death sentence to imprisonment for life.
issues.legal_principle: The choice of sentence requires an individualized assessment of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, including the offender’s role and the quality of the evidence establishing that role. The court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and, on the significance of evidence quality when considering death, Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Suresh v. State of U.P.

predicates.capital_sentencing_appeal: The case is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.conviction_for_murder_supported: The court upheld the offender’s murder conviction on the evidence supporting participation and common intention.
predicates.evidence_of_individual_role_insufficient: The evidence establishing the offender’s particular role was not sufficiently reliable or strong to justify the extreme sentence.

issues.definition: When a murder conviction is supported but the evidence about the offender’s individual role is insufficiently reliable for the extreme sentence, the death sentence is reduced to life imprisonment.

issues.legal_issue: A required sentencing hearing is satisfied when the court questions each convicted accused about sentence and considers the answers before choosing the punishment.
material_facts: After recording convictions, the trial court specifically questioned each accused about sentence and recorded the answers.
The trial court considered those answers along with the aggravating and mitigating circumstances before imposing sentence.
issues.conclusion: The court found no failure to comply with the sentencing-hearing requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires an opportunity to be heard on sentence after conviction. The court found the requirement met because the trial court questioned each accused and considered the responses in its sentencing decision.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.each_convicted_accused_heard_on_sentence: After conviction, the court asked each convicted accused to address the sentence.
predicates.sentencing_responses_considered: The court considered the accused persons’ responses when deciding the sentences.

issues.definition: The sentencing-hearing requirement is satisfied when each convicted accused is heard about sentence and the court considers the responses before imposing punishment.

issues.legal_issue: A remote possible influence from films and allegations of police corruption do not, without more, constitute mitigating circumstances for an offender who committed exceptionally brutal organized murders.
material_facts: The offender argued that films had influenced his conduct and that police misconduct had contributed to his criminal activities.
The court found that any possible influence from films was remote and that the allegations about police conduct did not mitigate the offender’s responsibility for the organized murders.
The court found that the offender had already become a hardened criminal and had committed the murders with extreme cruelty.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the asserted film influence and alleged police misconduct as mitigating circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Capital sentencing requires consideration of the offender’s circumstances, but a claimed circumstance must have a meaningful bearing on culpability or the appropriate sentence. Applying the sentencing approach in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, the court held that the remote influence alleged here and the asserted police conduct did not mitigate these crimes.

predicates.capital_sentencing_appeal: The case is an appeal in which the sentence is under review.
predicates.claimed_media_influence_remote: The offender claimed that media influenced the crimes, but the court found any influence remote.
predicates.alleged_police_misconduct_not_shown_to_m: The offender alleged police misconduct, but the court found it did not mitigate responsibility for the crimes.
predicates.offender_committed_extremely_cruel_organ: The offender committed organized murders in an exceptionally cruel manner.

issues.definition: In a sentencing appeal, remote claimed media influence and police misconduct that does not mitigate responsibility do not reduce punishment for exceptionally cruel organized murders.
